definition: A training approach that fine-tunes a model specifically to make better use of retrieved documents provided in its context, improving RAG system performance.
details: RAFT-style approaches train models to distinguish relevant from irrelevant retrieved passages and to cite evidence appropriately, addressing weaknesses that arise when a general-purpose model is simply given retrieved context at inference time without task-specific training.

explainer.lead: RAFT trains a model specifically to work well with retrieved documents in its context, rather than assuming a general model will use them well. It matters because standard RAG pipelines often stumble when the context is noisy or irrelevant.

tiers.eli5: Instead of just handing a student a pile of notes and hoping they use the right ones, you practice with them on piles that include junk, so they learn to pick out what matters.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers fine-tune on examples mixing relevant and irrelevant passages so the model learns to cite the right evidence and ignore distractors. A common pitfall is training only on clean contexts, which leaves the model fragile when real retrieval returns noise.
tiers.paperLevel: A supervised fine-tuning procedure where training examples pair a question with retrieved passages containing both relevant and distractor documents, and the target includes a reasoning chain plus citations to the relevant passages; performance is bounded by the quality and coverage of the retrieval corpus used in training.

explainer.example: A model is fine-tuned on questions where half the supplied passages are off-topic; at inference it learns to quote the two relevant documents and ignore the rest, improving answer accuracy over an untuned RAG baseline.
